searchText: Why AI Has to Get Lighter Efficient AI · Lecture 2 · Technology and engineering · Undergrad Why AI Has to Get Lighter Large models are capable but expensive to run. Lecture 2 names three levers that make them smaller and faster: fewer bits per weight, fewer weights, and hardware built for both. It then sets up the vocabulary Lecture 3 needs. Read the original slides ↗ The three paper links below were not retrieved in this session. Check them before relying on them. The lecture slides are the primary source for every claim tagged with a slide number. Bigger models work, but they cost more to run Large language models show emergent behaviors such as zero- and few-shot learning and chain-of-thought reasoning. [Lecture2, slide 6] [slide 8] [Wei et al., 2022] The catch is size: the capability "comes at the cost of large model size." [slide 7] Running that model on a laptop, a car, or a robot is hard. Those devices are resource-constrained and low-power, sometimes have no internet, and users do not want personal data uploaded to the cloud. [slide 13] The capability is cheap to ask for. Memory, speed and power are the bill. The lecture's worked example makes the trade concrete. LLaMA-2-7B runs at 50 tokens per second in FP16 and at 166 tokens per second with 4-bit weights and AWQ, about 3.3 times faster on a 4090 GPU. [slide 14] Quantization and pruning shrink the model, and hardware has to follow Quantization stores each weight in fewer bits. The slides name AWQ, which quantizes an LLM to 4-bit weights [AWQ, 2023] and also works on vision-language models. [slides 14, 18] SmoothQuant is cited for post-training quantization of LLMs. [slide 11] Pruning removes what the model does not need. SpAtten prunes redundant tokens. [slide 12] Full model FP32 or FP16 weights Quantize int8 or 4-bit Prune dense to sparse Hardware tensor cores, sparsity Runs on device faster, less power The software steps shrink the model. Only hardware that understands the smaller format turns that into speed. The hardware half is on slide 22. Single-chip inference performance rose 317 times in eight years, from the K20X at 3.94 Int8 TOPS to the A100 with structured sparsity at 1,248 TOPS. [slide 22] K20X 3.94 V100 125 Q8000 261 A100 (sparse) 1,248 Int8 TOPS per chip, as plotted on slide 22. The bars are linear, so the small values look tiny next to the A100. Cloud chips got much faster, and edge devices are still far behind Slide 24 tracks NVIDIA's data-center GPUs from 2016 to 2024. The table below reads those charts. Dense FP16 throughput grows from 18.7 to 1,750 TOPS while power stays near 700 W at the top end. [slide 24] Chip (year) Dense FP16 TOPS Memory bandwidth GB/s Power W Memory GB P100 (2016) 18.7 732 250 16 V100 (2017) 125 900 300 32 A100 (2020) 312 2,039 400 80 H100 (2022) 990 3,430 700 96 B100 (2024) 1,750 8,192 700 192 The slides close this section with the gap. Edge AI runs on a system-on-module or a microcontroller, which is a single chip with a processor, memory and I/O. [slides 27–28] The lecture's summary is that edge devices "still have huge gap to cloud processors." [slide 29] The vocabulary Lecture 3 builds on The slides set out three steps: review neural-network terms, review the building blocks, then introduce the efficiency metrics. [slide 33] The first building block is the fully connected layer, where every output neuron connects to every input. Written as one matrix multiply, it is Y = XWᵀ + b . [slide 36] y i = Σ j w ij x j + b i Each output is a weighted sum of its inputs, plus a bias. The slides use five features of a person, each weighted by how much it matters for a basketball team, as the example. [slide 37] The efficiency metrics the next lecture uses are parameter count, model size, peak activations, MACs, FLOPs, latency, and throughput. [slide 33] What this does not show The slides give benchmark numbers for specific models and chips at specific dates. They do not show the accuracy cost of 4-bit quantization or of pruning. The GPU table reproduces the lecture's charts and has not been checked against NVIDIA's datasheets. The 317-times figure on slide 22 is the lecture's own claim. The slides also give no numbers for phones compared with the cloud. Go deeper Read the Lecture 2 index in the cache folder for the slide-by-slide text, then move to Lecture 3, which covers the terminology and building blocks in full. [slides 33–40] For the original papers, start with the chain-of-thought paper, then AWQ and SmoothQuant. References Lecture 2, Efficient AI (local slides) Instructor's course slides, cited by slide number. Slide 1 credits materials drawn from Prof. Song Han's MIT course. AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for LLM Compression and Acceleration Lin et al., 2023. Named on slide 18. Source for 4-bit weight quantization. Not retrieved in this session. Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models Wei et al., 2022. Named on slides 8–10 as the source of chain-of-thought behavior. Not retrieved in this session. SmoothQuant: Accurate and Efficient Post-Training Quantization for Large Language Models ICML 2023. Named on slide 11. Post-training quantization for LLMs. Not retrieved in this session. searchText: Neural Network Building Blocks Technology · Efficient AI · CSC 4814/6814 · Lectures 2–3 Inside a Neural Network: Layers, Channels, and What They Cost A neural network is a stack of a few repeating building blocks: fully-connected layers, convolutions, pooling, normalization and activations. This page explains what each block computes and what its tensors look like. It spends extra time on the idea everything later depends on, the channel . Then it shows how to measure what a network costs in parameters, memory, latency and energy, which is the foundation for pruning and the rest of the course. Open the lecture slides ↗ Image 3 channels (RGB) Conv + ReLU filters → feature maps Pooling shrink height × width Fully-connected features → scores Output 1000 classes The path of one image through a typical CNN Predict first AlexNet has about 61 million parameters, and most of its layers are convolutions. Do you think most of the 61M parameters live in the conv layers or the fully-connected layers? And which kind of layer produces the most activations ? The answers are in section 7. 1 · Efficiency matters because models outgrew their hardware Deep learning is everywhere: vision, language, code generation, multimodal models and robots. Large language models even show emergent behaviors such as few-shot learning and chain-of-thought reasoning, but at the cost of enormous model size. The course goal is doing more with less: making AI fast, small and everywhere. [L2, motivation] The numbers show why. AWQ, a quantization method, speeds LLaMA-2-7B from 50 to 166 tokens/s on an RTX 4090, about 3.3× [AWQ, §5] . A robotics transformer runs at only 3 Hz because of its compute cost and network latency. Running models on the edge (phones, laptops, cars, robots) also keeps personal data private and works without internet. Edge hardware such as the Qualcomm Hexagon DSP, the Apple Neural Engine, NVIDIA Jetson and microcontrollers still has a huge gap to cloud processors. Efficiency rests on three pillars: algorithms, systems and hardware, each of which must support tricks like pruning and quantization. [L2, Three pillars] 2 · The vocabulary: synapses carry weights, neurons carry activations In the slides' 3-layer network (2 hidden layers), each connection is a synapse , also called a weight or parameter. Each circle is a neuron , also called a feature or activation. A neuron takes inputs x i , multiplies each by its weight w i , adds a bias b , and passes the sum through an activation function f : [L3, Recap DNN] y = f( Σ i w i x i + b ) Word Same thing as Is it learned? Synapse weight, parameter Yes, stored in the model file Neuron feature, activation No, computed fresh for every input Width size of the hidden layers A design choice Keep this split in mind: weights are what the model is , and activations are what it produces while running. Section 7 shows that these two cost memory in very different ways. 3 · A fully-connected layer is one matrix multiply Every output neuron connects to every input neuron. The slides' intuition: think of x as 5 features of a person (height, weight, age…). To score "fits a basketball team," you weight each feature by how much it matters, add them up, and shift by a bias: [L2–3, One neuron] y 0 = w 00 x 0 + w 01 x 1 + w 02 x 2 + w 03 x 3 + w 04 x 4 + b 0 →  y i = Σ j w ij x j + b i Stack all the output neurons and the whole layer collapses into Y = XW T + b: one matrix multiply, plus a bias. Tensor Shape Meaning Input X (n, c i ) n samples in the batch, c i input channels (features) Output Y (n, c o ) c o output channels Weights W (c o , c i ) one row per output neuron Bias b (c o ,) one per output neuron Notice the word channels already: in a linear layer, a "channel" is simply one feature. For a single sample, the shapes are (1, c i ) and (1, c o ). Stacking two such layers gives a multilayer perceptron (MLP). Each output neuron does c i multiply-accumulates (MACs), so the layer does c i ·c o MACs . [L4, #MACs] 4 · A channel is one "view" of the input, and every filter makes one Here is the idea that the pruning lectures assume you know. Start with a color photo. It is not one grid of numbers but three : a red grid, a green grid and a blue grid stacked on top of each other. Each of those grids is a channel . An RGB image has c i = 3 channels, each h × w pixels. [L3, 2D conv, RGB split] A convolution slides a small kernel (for example 3×3) over the image and computes a weighted sum at every location. The kernel decides what you see. The same photo with four different 3×3 kernels gives four different results: [L3, The kernel decides] Lab 1 · Slide a 3×3 kernel over a 6×6 image Identity Edge detect Blur Sharpen Input (1 channel) Kernel Output feature map Now the key step. A conv layer does not learn one kernel; it learns many filters , and each filter outputs its own channel . In the slides, a 3-channel cat photo goes through N learned filters and comes out as N output maps. One map highlights edges, another fur texture, another outlines. Those output maps are the layer's output channels , also called feature maps . [L3, One filter, one feature map] Input c i channels, h i ×w i c o filters each c i ×k h ×k w Output c o channels, h o ×w o Filter j looks at all c i input channels at once and produces output channel j Since the input has c i channels, each filter is really a stack of c i kernels, one per input channel. The filter applies each kernel to its channel and adds the results into a single output map. That is why the weight tensor has the shape W : (c o , c i , k h , k w ) with one k×k kernel for every (output channel, input channel) pair. In the slide, c i = 3 (RGB) and c o = N, the number of learned filters. [L3, Weight tensor shape] Why channels are the natural unit for pruning Deleting output channel j of a layer removes three things at once: Filter j in this layer: c i ·k h ·k w weights. Feature map j : h o ·w o activations that no longer need to be computed or stored. The matching slice of every filter in the next layer . That layer's input now has one channel fewer, so each of its filters loses one k×k kernel. What is left is an ordinary, smaller dense convolution, so every library and chip runs it faster with no special support. That is the "direct speedup" in the pruning slides. Fine-grained pruning, by contrast, leaves scattered zeros inside a tensor of the same shape. Try it: Lab 2 · Prune channels between two conv layers (56×56 maps, 3×3 kernels) Layer A: 64 → 128 channels  ·  Layer B: 128 → 256 channels Drag the slider to keep 64 of the 128 middle channels. Layer A's weights halve, the feature maps between the layers halve, and Layer B's weights also halve, even though you never touched Layer B's own output. One decision saves memory in two layers. It also explains the pruning lecture's warning that channel pruning has a smaller compression ratio : you can only remove whole channels, never the single weakest weights. 5 · Convolution variants: same idea, different shapes In a conv layer, each output neuron connects only to the input neurons in its receptive field , not to everything. In 1D convolution the kernel slides along one dimension, such as time in an ECG signal, and learns temporal patterns. In 2D convolution it slides along height and width, such as detecting a stop sign in a street scene, and learns spatial patterns like edges, textures and shapes. [L3, 1D vs 2D] Tensor Linear 1D conv 2D conv Input X (n, c i ) (n, c i , w i ) (n, c i , h i , w i ) Output Y (n, c o ) (n, c o , w o ) (n, c o , h o , w o ) Weights W (c o , c i ) (c o , c i , k w ) (c o , c i , k h , k w ) Bias b (c o ,) (c o ,) (c o ,) Notation: n batch size · c i /c o input/output channels · h, w height/width · k h , k w kernel height/width · g groups. Stride is how far the kernel jumps between positions. On the slide's 7×7 input with a 3×3 kernel, stride 1 visits all 25 positions (a 5×5 output), while stride 2 visits only 9 (a 3×3 output). The slides don't give a general formula, but the standard one, with padding p zeros added around the border, is: [Dumoulin & Visin, §2] h o = ⌊(h i + 2p − k h ) / s⌋ + 1 Check it against AlexNet's first layer (224 input, 11×11 kernel, stride 4, pad 2): ⌊(224 + 4 − 11)/4⌋ + 1 = 55. That matches the 96×55×55 output in the slides. Grouped convolution splits the channels into g groups, and each group is a narrower convolution that sees only its own c i /g input channels. The weights shrink from (c o , c i , k h , k w ) to (g·c o /g, c i /g, k h , k w ), which is g times fewer . Depthwise convolution is the extreme case g = c i = c o . Every channel gets its own independent filter and channels never mix, so W is just (c, k h , k w ). Efficient mobile networks like MobileNetV2 are built on this. [MobileNetV2, §3.1] Lab 3 · Conv layer calculator. Try the presets, then your own numbers. AlexNet conv1 AlexNet conv2 (g=2) AlexNet conv5 (g=2) Depthwise 3×3 6 · The supporting layers have few or no parameters Pooling downsamples a feature map. Each output neuron pools the features in its receptive field, like convolution, and the stride usually equals the kernel size (s = k). Pooling works on each channel independently and has no learnable parameters . [L3, Pooling] Lab 4 · 2×2 pooling, stride 2 (the slide's example) Max pooling Average pooling Input 4×4 Output 2×2 Hover over an output cell to see the 2×2 window it came from. Normalization makes optimization faster. Each feature is shifted and scaled using the mean μ i and standard deviation σ i over a set of pixels S i : [Wu & He, §3.1] x̂ i = (x i − μ i ) / σ i ,   μ i = (1/m) Σ k∈S i x k ,   σ i = √( (1/m) Σ k∈S i (x k − μ i )² + ε ) Then a per-channel linear transform with a trainable scale γ and shift β, y i = γ x̂ i + β, restores the representational ability that normalization might remove. The variants differ only in which set S i they average over: Variant Statistics computed over Batch Norm One channel, across the whole batch and all pixels Layer Norm One sample, across all channels and pixels Instance Norm One sample, one channel Group Norm One sample, one group of channels Look back at the pruning page: scaling-based pruning reuses exactly this per-channel γ. A channel with a tiny γ is barely let through, so it can be cut. Activation functions are typically non-linear, and most common activation functions have no learnable parameters. [L3, Activation] Name Formula Sigmoid y = 1/(1 + e −x ) ReLU y = max(0, x) ReLU6 y = min(max(0, x), 6) Leaky ReLU y = max(αx, x) Swish y = x/(1 + e −x ) Hard Swish 0 if x ≤ −3; x if x ≥ 3; x(x + 3)/6 otherwise Others include Tanh, GELU, ELU and Mish. ReLU's flat zero region is what creates the zeros that APoZ pruning counts. Putting it together. The slides' CNN example (VGG-style) shrinks space while growing channels: 224×224×64 → 112×112×128 → 56×56×256 → 28×28×512 → 14×14×512 → 7×7×512, then fully-connected layers of 4096, 4096 and 1000. Each stage is conv + ReLU, with max pooling between stages. [Simonyan & Zisserman, Table 1] 7 · Efficiency has more than one meaning The slides draw a triangle. Storage makes models smaller, latency makes them faster, and energy makes them greener, and both computation and memory sit in the middle and drive all three. The metrics come in two families: [L3, Efficiency metrics] Memory-related Computation-related #parameters · model size · total / peak #activations MAC · FLOP, FLOPS · OP, OPS Latency and throughput are not the same Latency is the delay for one task. For example, SegFormer takes 638 ms per frame (82.4 mIoU), while EfficientViT takes 46 ms (82.7 mIoU). Throughput is the rate at which data is processed, for example 6.1 vs 77.4 videos per second. [L3, Latency, Throughput] Puzzle from the slides Design 1 handles one image at a time in 50 ms. Design 2 handles 4 images in parallel, taking 100 ms each. Which has lower latency? Which has higher throughput? Answer Design 1 has 50 ms latency and 20 images/s throughput. Design 2 has 100 ms latency but 40 images/s throughput. Higher throughput does not imply lower latency, and lower latency does not imply higher throughput. Parallelism buys throughput; making each job faster buys latency. Latency is roughly set by whichever is slower, computing or moving data: Latency ≈ max(T computation , T memory ) Term ≈ NN specification ÷ hardware specification T computation #operations in the model #operations the processor does per second T data movement of weights model size memory bandwidth T data movement of activations input + output activation size memory bandwidth where T memory ≈ T activations + T weights . Every term is a model number divided by a hardware number. You can make a model faster by shrinking the top line, which is what pruning does, or by buying a better bottom line. Energy: moving data is what costs Rough energy per operation at 45 nm, 0.9 V. Each bar's length is on a log scale: [Horowitz, Fig. 1.1.9] A single DRAM access costs about 200× a 32-bit multiply. Data movement means more memory references, and that means more energy. This is why the pruning lectures care about removing activations , not just multiplies. Counting parameters #Parameters is the number of elements in the weight tensors. Ignoring bias: [L3, #Parameters] Layer #Parameters Linear c o ·c i Convolution c o ·c i ·k h ·k w Grouped convolution (c o /g)·(c i /g)·k h ·k w ·g = c o ·c i ·k h ·k w /g Depthwise convolution c o ·k h ·k w Model size is the storage for the weights. When the whole network uses one data type, model size = #parameters × bit width. For AlexNet's 61M parameters, 32-bit floats take 61M × 4 bytes ≈ 244 MB, and 8-bit integers take 61M × 1 byte = 61 MB. That 4× saving is the promise of quantization. AlexNet, counted by hand Here is the predict-first answer. Work down the table; the one "?" is yours to fill in: [Krizhevsky et al., Fig. 2] Layer Output C×H×W #Parameters #Activations Image 3×224×224 – 150,528 11×11 conv, 96, s4, p2 96×55×55 96·3·11·11 = 34,848 290,400 3×3 maxpool, s2 96×27×27 0 69,984 5×5 conv, 256, p2, g2 256×27×27 256·96·5·5/2 = 307,200 186,624 3×3 maxpool, s2 256×13×13 0 43,264 3×3 conv, 384, p1 384×13×13 384·256·3·3 = 884,736 64,896 3×3 conv, 384, p1, g2 384×13×13 384·384·3·3/2 = 663,552 64,896 3×3 conv, 256, p1, g2 256×13×13 ? (try it) 256·384·3·3/2 = 442,368 43,264 3×3 maxpool, s2 256×6×6 0 9,216 Linear 4096 4096 4096·(256·6·6) = 37,748,736 4,096 Linear 4096 4096 4096·4096 = 16,777,216 4,096 Linear 1000 1000 1000·4096 = 4,096,000 1,000 The totals are about 61M parameters and 932,264 activations . Now look at where each one sits. The three linear layers hold 58.6M of the 61M parameters (about 96% ), yet produce only 9,192 activations. The first conv layer has just 34,848 parameters but produces the most activations of any layer. Weights pile up at the end of a CNN, and activations pile up at the start. The peak activation memory is roughly the largest input + output pair: 150,528 + 290,400 = 440,928 . [L3, AlexNet #Activations] Activations, not parameters, are often the real bottleneck Inference (int8): at about 70% ImageNet top-1, MobileNetV2-0.75 has 4.6× fewer parameters than ResNet-18, but a 1.8× higher peak activation. [MCUNet, Fig. 2] Imbalance: MobileNetV2's memory peaks at 1,372 kB in block 2, far above a 256 kB microcontroller limit, while later blocks need little. Training (fp32): MobileNetV2-1.4 has 4.3× fewer parameters than ResNet-50 (102 MB), but its activations shrink only 1.1×. ResNet-50's activations (707 MB) are about 7× larger than its parameters. [TinyTL, Fig. 1] Per layer: early layers have high activation memory, and late layers have high weight memory. It is the same pattern you just found in AlexNet. Concept map Needs first Weighted sum Matrix multiply Image as grid This topic NN building blocks Channel Conv / grouped / depthwise Pool, norm, activation Efficiency metrics Leads to Pruning Quantization Edge deployment From Relation To Fully-connected layer formalized-by Y = XW T + b Filter causes one output channel Channel part-of activation tensor (n, c, h, w) Depthwise conv is-a grouped conv with g = c i = c o Latency contrasts-with throughput Model size measured-by #params × bit width Data movement causes most energy cost Channel pruning requires understanding filters and feature maps Exam check: try before you open A conv layer has 32 input channels, 64 output channels and 3×3 kernels. Write W's shape and count the parameters. Answer W : (64, 32, 3, 3), so 64·32·9 = 18,432 parameters (plus 64 biases). The same layer with g = 4 groups. And as depthwise (assume c i = c o = 32)? Answer Grouped: 18,432/4 = 4,608. Depthwise: 32·9 = 288. Input 3×32×32, 5×5 conv, stride 1, padding 0, 16 filters. What is the output shape? Answer (32 − 5)/1 + 1 = 28, so the output is 16×28×28. The output channel count always equals the number of filters. A model has 25M parameters. What is its model size in fp32 and in int8? Answer fp32: 25M × 4 B = 100 MB. int8: 25 MB. Why can't you judge a CNN's memory needs from #parameters alone? Answer Activations often dominate, especially in early layers and during training. Example: MobileNetV2 has 4.6× fewer parameters than ResNet-18 but a 1.8× higher peak activation. Does pooling add parameters? Does ReLU? Does BatchNorm? Answer Pooling has none. ReLU has none. BatchNorm has two per channel, the trainable γ and β. If you prune 25% of the output channels of layer L, which other layer's weights shrink, and by how much? Answer Layer L+1. Its input channels drop by 25%, so its weights shrink by 25% too. Layer L's own weights also drop by 25%, along with the feature maps between the two layers. What this does not show The slides list Transformers as a building block, but Lectures 2–3 have no slides on them, so this page skips them. MAC/FLOP counting for conv layers belongs to Lecture 4. The calculator in Lab 3 shows MACs only as a preview. The output-size formula comes from a standard reference rather than the slides. All benchmark numbers depend on the hardware and setup named next to them. References CSC 4814/6814 Efficient AI, Lectures 2–3 (Dr. Haoxin Wang, GSU) The course slides this page follows: terminology, FC and conv layers, channels, pooling, normalization, activations, efficiency metrics and AlexNet counts. Lecture 2 and Lecture 4 (#MACs) are in the same folder. Krizhevsky et al., ImageNet Classification with Deep CNNs (NeurIPS 2012) The AlexNet architecture behind the parameter and activation tables. Dumoulin & Visin, A guide to convolution arithmetic for deep learning (2016) The output-size formula with stride and padding. Horowitz, Computing's Energy Problem (and what we can do about it) (ISSCC 2014) The energy-per-operation table and the cost of DRAM access. Lin et al., MCUNet: Tiny Deep Learning on IoT Devices (NeurIPS 2020) Peak activation vs parameters, MobileNetV2's imbalanced memory, and per-layer memory distribution. Cai et al., TinyTL: Reduce Activations, Not Trainable Parameters (NeurIPS 2020) Activations as the memory bottleneck in training. Wu & He, Group Normalization (ECCV 2018) The normalization formula and the Batch, Layer, Instance and Group Norm comparison. Sandler et al., MobileNetV2: Inverted Residuals and Linear Bottlenecks (CVPR 2018) Depthwise (separable) convolution in an efficient mobile network. Simonyan & Zisserman, Very Deep Convolutional Networks (VGG, ICLR 2015) The CNN architecture example with its shrinking spatial size and growing channel counts. Lin et al., AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization (MLSys 2024) The LLaMA-2 speedup example (50 → 166 tokens/s on an RTX 4090). searchText: Counting What Makes a Network Expensive Efficient AI · Lecture 3 · Technology and engineering · Undergrad · Deep Counting What Makes a Network Expensive Most people count parameters and assume that is the cost of a network. Lecture 3 shows that the number that usually bites is memory for activations, and that speed and throughput are different measures. It then builds the convolution layer that produces both. Read the original slides ↗ The arXiv link below was not retrieved in this session, and the publisher links are top-level pages. Check them before relying on them. Every claim tagged with a slide number comes from the lecture slides, and the figure readings were taken from the PNG renders. Parameters are not the memory bill A network's parameter count is the number of weights and biases it stores. The lecture's first efficiency claim is that this number is not what limits inference. The slides say that #Activations, not #Parameters, is the memory bottleneck in CNN inference, and the same holds in training. [Lecture3, slides 44, 46] Weights sit in storage once. Activations are rebuilt for every input, and a single layer's activations must fit in memory at the same time. The rest of this page follows that idea. It counts parameters, counts activations, and then shows what happens when the memory limit is a microcontroller's 256 kB. [slide 45] Latency and throughput answer different questions The slides define latency as the delay for one specific task, and throughput as the rate at which data is processed. [slides 32–33] They then compare two designs for the same workload, four images at 100 ms each. Design 1 processes one image at a time, and Design 2 runs four in parallel. [slide 34] Design Images in parallel Latency Throughput Design 1 1 50 ms 20 images/s Design 2 4 100 ms 40 images/s The two measures matter for different products. A camera app that must answer one frame quickly cares about latency. A job that labels a large batch of photos overnight cares about throughput. The slide's example is designed to show that the two can move in opposite directions, so a design chosen for one may be wrong for the other. This paragraph is general reasoning, not a result from the slides. Design 2 doubles throughput while making each image wait twice as long. Higher throughput does not mean lower latency here. The slide asks both questions, "does higher throughput translate to lower latency?" and "does lower latency translate to higher throughput?", and the answer depends on the design. [slide 34] A model that is fast for one input can still be slow overall, and the reverse is also true. Counting parameters means counting weight tensors Every layer stores a weight tensor. For a convolution the slides write its shape as W : (c o , c i , k, k) , one k×k kernel for each pair of output and input channels. [slide 17] The same counting rule gives the parameter count for each layer type. [slides 38–40] Layer #Parameters Linear c o · c i Convolution c o · c i · k h · k w Grouped convolution c o · c i · k h · k w / g Depthwise convolution c o · k h · k w AlexNet, the slides' worked example, has about 61 million parameters in total, with bias ignored. [slide 48] The three linear layers hold most of them. The 4096 × 9216 layer alone has 37.7 million weights. The three together hold about 58.6 million of the 61 million, or 96%. The convolution layers are small by comparison. Linear 1 (4096 × 256·6·6) 37.7M Linear 2 (4096 × 4096) 16.8M Linear 3 (1000 × 4096) 4.1M All other layers ~2.4M AlexNet parameters by layer group, from slide 48. The last row is the 61M total minus the three linear layers, so it is approximate because the slide rounds the total. The formulas also show how design choices move the count. In every row the output channel count c o is a multiplier, so doubling it doubles the parameters of that layer. Grouping by g divides the count by g relative to a dense convolution with the same channels. These are direct readings of the table, not measured results. [slides 38–40] Because the parameter count is dominated by linear layers, it says little about the memory a convolutional network needs while it runs. That is the lecture's reason for counting activations separately. Counting activations means counting what must be held at once An activation is the output a layer produces for one input. For AlexNet the slides count 150,528 values in the input image (3 × 224 × 224), 290,400 in the first convolution's output (96 × 55 × 55), and 932,264 in total across all layers. [slide 49] The peak is roughly the input plus the output of the largest step: 150,528 + 290,400 = 440,928 values. [slide 49] A flow diagram makes the difference clear. Weights are read from storage, activations are created and destroyed for each input, and the peak has to fit the device. One layer input and weights Weights #Parameters, stored once Activations #Activations, per input Peak memory input + output of the step Device limit RAM on the chip Weights are fixed. Activations are the working memory. The peak has to fit under the limit. The arithmetic makes the point. The first AlexNet convolution's output, 290,400 values, is about 1.9 times the input image's 150,528 values. That layer has far fewer parameters than the first linear layer, which holds 37.7 million. Memory cost follows the shape of the feature map, which depends on the spatial size and channel count, rather than the parameter count. [slides 48, 49] On a microcontroller, the peak layer decides everything The MCUNet work on IoT devices shows where memory actually goes. For MobileNetV2 the slides plot memory per block. Block 2 peaks at 1,372 kB, while the microcontroller limit is 256 kB. [slide 45] However few parameters the model has, a 256 kB device cannot hold that block's peak memory. Peak, block 2 1,372 kB MCU limit 256 kB MobileNetV2 peak block memory against the microcontroller constraint, from slide 45. The MCU limit is about 19% of the peak. The per-layer view in MCUNet shows the pattern more fully. Early layers have high activation memory, late layers have high weight memory, and the middle layers have low memory cost in both. [slide 47] A design that balances the two is what makes a network fit. Convolution is where both numbers come from A convolution slides a small kernel over the input and computes a weighted sum at each position. [slide 14] That is the weighted-sum neuron from Lecture 2, repeated across space. Slide 14 shows one photo filtered by four different 3×3 kernels, edge detection, blur, and sharpen among them, giving four different features. Each kernel is a small set of weights, so one convolution layer holds many filters, and each filter produces one output channel. [slides 14, 17] Stride controls how many positions the kernel visits. On a 5×5 grid, stride 1 visits 25 positions, while stride 2 visits 9. [slide 22] A 1D convolution slides along one dimension, such as time, and a 2D convolution slides along height and width. [slide 12] Grouped and depthwise convolutions reduce the parameter count, by dividing by g or dropping the input-channel factor. The table above shows both. [slides 23–24] Pooling shrinks a 4×4 map to 2×2. [slide 25] Most common activation functions have no learnable parameters. [slide 27] Which number is the bottleneck? Before optimizing, ask which resource is short. If the model must fit in storage, the weight count is the question, and the linear layers of AlexNet are where to look. If the model must fit in RAM, the question is the peak activation step, as in the MobileNetV2 figure. If the model must answer quickly, the question is latency for one input, and if it must process a large queue, the question is throughput. The same network can be fine on one of these and fail on another. This checklist is a reading of the lecture's framing, not a method the slides state in one place. How the ideas connect Needs first Weighted sum Convolution kernel This topic Efficiency of neural networks #Parameters #Activations Latency Throughput Model size Leads to Tiny deep learning on MCUs From Relation To Convolution requires Weighted sum #Parameters part-of Efficiency of neural networks #Activations part-of Efficiency of neural networks Latency part-of Efficiency of neural networks Throughput part-of Efficiency of neural networks Model size part-of Efficiency of neural networks Latency contrasts-with Throughput #Activations contrasts-with #Parameters #Activations applied-in Tiny deep learning on MCUs What this does not show The text layer for slides 30 to 43 is mostly titles, so the energy consumption and model size slides (36 and 42) were not read in detail and no numbers are given for them here. The slides give no accuracy figures for any of the networks, so the trade-offs above are about cost, not quality. The latency and throughput example is a teaching case with four images and fixed times, not a measurement. The MCU figures come from one paper and one device limit. Go deeper Start with the Lecture 2 page for the hardware and quantization side of the same argument. [Lecture 2 page] Then return to the slides in order: the counting rules at slides 38 to 40, the AlexNet worked example at 48 and 49, and the MCU figures at 45 and 47. searchText: Neural Network Pruning Technology · Efficient AI · CSC 4814/6814 · Lectures 4–6 Neural Network Pruning: Cutting a Model Without Killing It Most weights in a trained network contribute almost nothing. Pruning removes them and leaves a smaller, faster model that is nearly as accurate. Doing it well means answering four questions: what unit to cut, which ones to cut, how much to cut in each layer, and how to recover afterward. This page walks through all four, with small labs where you can try each idea yourself. Open the lecture slides ↗ Dense model trained, oversized Granularity what unit? Criterion which ones? Ratio how much per layer? Fine-tune recover accuracy The four decisions of pruning, in the order the lectures cover them Predict first A trained AlexNet has 61 million weights. How many do you think you could delete with no loss in accuracy: 10%, 50% or 90%? Keep your guess in mind; the answer is in section 6. 1 · Pruning is an optimization problem with a budget The slides start with an analogy: pruning is like trimming a tree. You cut away the branches that are not pulling their weight, and the tree keeps its shape, stays healthy, and grows back stronger. In a network, the branches are weights. The human brain does the same thing: it first grows many connections, then removes the less useful ones as it develops. [L4–5, intro slides] You can prune two kinds of things. Synapses are the weights (parameters) on the connections. Neurons are the activations: the outputs of the units themselves. Removing synapses means fewer parameters and less computation. Removing neurons means fewer activations and less data movement, which matters because moving data in memory costs far more energy than doing arithmetic. [L4, Memory is expensive] Formally, pruning finds the best pruned weights W P under a hard budget: arg min W P L(x; W P )   subject to   ‖W P ‖ 0 < N Here L is the training objective, x is the input, W are the original weights and W P the pruned ones. ‖·‖ 0 counts the nonzero entries, and N is the target number of nonzeros. Out of all possible weight values, find the ones that make the prediction error smallest, but you may keep at most N of them nonzero. Every method below is a different way to approximate this problem, because solving it exactly would mean trying every possible subset of weights. [L5–6, formulation] 2 · Granularity trades flexibility for real speed Granularity is the unit you remove: a single weight, a group of weights, or an entire channel or filter. Start with a 3×3 weight matrix. Fine-grained (unstructured) pruning may zero any entry, for example keeping only w 11 , w 13 , w 22 , w 31 and w 33 . Coarse-grained (structured) pruning removes whole rows, so what remains is simply a smaller dense matrix. [L5, 2D weight matrix] Fine-grained / unstructured Coarse-grained / structured Index choice Most flexible Less flexible: a subset of the fine-grained choices Hardware Hard to accelerate (irregular) Easy to accelerate: just a smaller matrix Lab 1 · Same matrix, same 50% budget, three granularities Dense Fine-grained 50% 2:4 pattern Row (structured) Try each button. Every mode keeps exactly 16 of 32 weights, yet the share of total weight magnitude kept falls as the pattern becomes more regular. The more structure you demand, the more good weights you are forced to throw away. In exchange, the hardware gets something it can actually run faster. New to channels? A conv layer's weights have shape (c o , c i , k h , k w ), where each output channel is one feature map made by one filter. If that sentence is fuzzy, read What is a channel? on the companion page first, and try its channel-pruning lab. Everything below will make more sense. The spectrum for convolutional layers A conv weight tensor has four dimensions: output channels c o , input channels c i , kernel height k h and kernel width k w . The slide's example uses 3×3 kernels with c i = 2. Going from irregular to regular, the common granularities are: fine-grained (any single weight), pattern-based (fixed shapes, "like Tetris"), vector-level (a row of a kernel), kernel-level (a whole k h × k w kernel) and channel-level (a whole channel). [Mao et al., Fig. 1] Granularity Pro Con Fine-grained Flexible indices, usually the largest compression ratio Needs special hardware to turn sparsity into speed Pattern (N:M) Supported on NVIDIA Ampere GPUs, about 2× speedup, accuracy kept Fixed 50% sparsity for 2:4 Vector / kernel More regular than fine-grained Less flexible Channel Direct speedup: the result is just a thinner network Smallest compression ratio Fine-grained in numbers. Because the redundant weights can be chosen freely, the compression is large: [Han et al., Table 1–4] Network Before After Reduction AlexNet 61 M 6.7 M 9× VGG-16 138 M 10.3 M 12× GoogleNet 7 M 2.0 M 3.5× ResNet50 26 M 7.47 M 3.4× Look at which networks compress least. GoogleNet and ResNet50 were already designed to be lean, so they have less fat to cut. N:M sparsity. In every M contiguous elements, N are pruned. The classic case is 2:4, which is 50% sparsity. There are C(4,2) = 6 ways to choose which two survive, so each kept value needs only a 2-bit index . The compressed matrix stores half the values plus those indices. NVIDIA's Ampere architecture runs this at up to about 2× speed. Accuracy is maintained on a wide range of tasks: [Mishra et al., §4] Network Metric Dense FP16 2:4 sparse ResNet-50 Top-1 76.1 76.2 ResNeXt-101 32x8d Top-1 79.3 79.3 Xception Top-1 79.2 79.2 SSD-RN50 bbAP 24.8 24.8 MaskRCNN-RN50 bbAP 37.9 37.9 FairSeq Transformer BLEU 28.2 28.5 BERT-Large F1 91.9 91.9 Channel pruning. Removing whole channels gives a direct speedup, because the network simply has fewer channels, but the compression ratio is smaller. Pruning every layer by the same 0.3 ("uniform shrink") does worse than giving each layer its own sparsity, for example 0.5, 0.3, 0.7, 0.2, 0.3. On ImageNet, channel pruning with AMC reaches higher accuracy at every latency than uniform scaling does. How to find those per-layer numbers is section 5. [He et al. 2018, Fig. 1] 3 · To pick weights, ask "how much would the loss notice?" The rule: the less important the removed parameters are, the better the pruned network performs. Try it on one neuron: y = ReLU(10 x 0 − 8 x 1 + 0.1 x 2 ). If you must delete one weight, which one? [L5, Selection of synapses] Answer The 0.1. Removing it changes y the least, because its input is scaled down to almost nothing. That intuition is the whole idea behind magnitude-based pruning. Method 1 · Magnitude-based (heuristic) Weights with larger absolute values are treated as more important. For element-wise pruning, importance = | w |. For structured pruning, you measure the magnitude of a whole group S (such as a row) with the L p -norm: [Han et al., §3] ‖W (S) ‖ p = ( Σ i∈S |w i | p ) 1/p Use p = 1 for the row-wise L1 norm (Σ| w i |) and p = 2 for the L2 norm ( √Σ| w i |² ). Lab 2 · Magnitude pruning at 50%. Edit the weights. Element-wise |w| Row-wise L1 Row-wise L2 Weight Importance Pruned weight With the slide's example [[3, −2], [1, −5]], element-wise pruning keeps 3 and −5. Row-wise L1 gives the rows importance 5 and 6, and L2 gives √13 and √26. Either norm kills row 0, leaving [[0, 0], [1, −5]]. Now change −2 to −4 and see whether L1 and L2 still agree. [L5, Method 1 examples] Method 2 · Scaling-based (for filters) Each filter (output channel) of a conv layer gets a trainable scaling factor γ, which multiplies that channel's output. After training, channels with small γ are pruned. In the slide, filters with factors 0.10 and 0.29 are removed, while those with 1.17, 0.82 and 0.56 survive. Instead of guessing importance afterward, the network learns it during training. [Liu et al., §3] Method 3 · Second-order (Optimal Brain Damage) The goal here is to minimize the increase in loss caused by pruning. Expand that increase with a Taylor series: [LeCun et al., §2] δL = L(x;W) − L(x;W P = W − δW) = Σ i g i δw i + ½Σ i h ii δw i 2 + ½Σ i≠j h ij δw i δw j + O(‖δW‖ 3 ) where g i = ∂L/∂w i and h ij = ∂²L/∂w i ∂w j . Optimal Brain Damage assumes three things, and each one deletes a term: Assumption Term removed L is nearly quadratic O(‖δW‖³), the last term Training has converged Σ g i δw i , the first-order term (the gradient is about 0) Deleting each parameter has an independent effect The cross terms h ij , i ≠ j δL i = L(x;W) − L(x;W P | w i = 0) ≈ ½ h ii w i 2 This is the estimated increase in loss if w i is set to zero. Build the intuition: if every h ii were equal, ranking by ½ h ii w i ² would be the same as ranking by | w i |. Magnitude pruning is the special case that ignores curvature. OBD's extra contribution is noticing that a small weight sitting in a steep direction of the loss can matter more than a large weight in a flat one. 4 · To pick neurons, watch them while they work Removing a neuron removes a whole row of the weight matrix in a linear layer, or a whole channel in a conv layer. Neuron pruning is coarse-grained weight pruning. The rule is the same as before: the less useful the removed neurons are, the better the pruned network performs. [L5–6, Selection of neurons] Percentage-of-zero (APoZ) ReLU outputs zero for every negative input. A channel that is almost always zero is barely contributing. The Average Percentage of Zeros (APoZ) of a channel counts its zero activations over a batch. The smaller the APoZ, the more important the neuron. [Hu et al., §3] Lab 3 · The slide's activations: batch of 2, 3 channels, 4×4 each Your turn Count the zeros per channel across both inputs, then decide which channel to prune. Highlight zeros + compute APoZ One practical catch: APoZ depends on data, so you must actually run a few inferences to measure it. Weight magnitude, by contrast, can be read straight from the model file. [L5, APoZ] Regression-based (layer reconstruction) Instead of tracking the network's final loss L (x; W), this method minimizes the reconstruction error of one layer's outputs . That is a smaller, local problem. Split the layer's matrix product by input channel: [He et al. 2017, §3.1] Z = XW T = Σ c=0 c i −1 X c W c T arg min W,β ‖Z − Ẑ‖ F 2 = ‖Z − Σ c β c X c W c T ‖ F 2 s.t.   ‖β‖ 0 ≤ N c β is a coefficient vector of length c i that selects channels: β c = 0 means channel c is pruned. N c is the number of nonzero channels. Solve it by alternating : fix W and solve for β to choose channels, then fix β and solve for W to minimize the reconstruction error. In other words, after removing channels, the remaining weights adjust to make up for them. 5 · Each layer needs its own ratio Non-uniform pruning beats uniform shrinking because layers differ in sensitivity . Some, like the first layer, are fragile; others are highly redundant. [He et al. 2018, §1] Sensitivity analysis (VGG-11 on CIFAR-10) Pick a layer L i . Prune only that layer, at ratios r ∈ {0, 0.1, …, 0.9} (or other strides), and record the accuracy drop ΔAcc r i . Repeat for every layer. Pick a degradation threshold T that gives the overall pruning rate you want. Each layer's ratio is the largest r whose accuracy stays above T . Lab 4 · Drag the threshold T and read off per-layer ratios Threshold T = 80 % accuracy Curves traced by eye from the slide's VGG-11/CIFAR-10 plot. They're for building intuition, not exact values. Is this optimal? Probably not, because sensitivity analysis tests each layer alone and ignores how layers interact. Pruning L3 changes what L4 receives. Conventionally, filling this gap takes human expertise and many rounds of trial and error. Can we push a button instead? [L6, Finding pruning ratios] AMC: pruning as reinforcement learning AMC (AutoML for Model Compression) replaces the human with an agent that works through the network one layer at a time. [He et al. 2018, §3] State s layer idx, N, C, H, W, kernel, FLOPs… DDPG agent actor + critic Action a ∈ [0,1) sparsity of layer t Reward −Error, or −∞ The agent compresses layer t, sees the result, moves to t+1 Action is a continuous ratio, which is why they use DDPG: it supports continuous actions. Reward R = −Error if the result satisfies the constraints, and −∞ if not. A variant uses −Error·log(FLOP). Latency constraints are handled with a pre-built lookup table (LUT) of measured layer latencies. On ResNet50, AMC finds sparser layers than a human expert. Density is the share of nonzero weights, so lower is better: Conv1 43 vs 50 ResBlock1 28 vs 31 ResBlock2 28 vs 31 ResBlock3 23 vs 30 ResBlock4 19 vs 30 FC 10 vs 20 Total 20 vs 29 AMC density % (bar) vs human expert % On MobileNet, measured with TF-Lite on a Samsung Galaxy S7 Edge (Snapdragon SoC, single core, batch size 1): [He et al. 2018, Table 5] Model MAC Top-1 Latency Speedup Memory 1.0 MobileNet 569M 70.6% 119.0 ms 1× 20.1 MB AMC (50% FLOPs) 285M 70.5% 64.4 ms 1.8× 14.3 MB AMC (50% Time) 272M 70.2% 59.7 ms 2.0× 13.2 MB 0.75 MobileNet 325M 68.4% 69.5 ms 1.7× 14.8 MB Compare the last two rows. AMC (50% Time) is faster than the hand-shrunk 0.75 MobileNet and 1.8 points more accurate, because it chose where to cut instead of shrinking everything evenly. NetAdapt: a rule-based iterative method The goal is the same: find per-layer ratios that meet a global resource constraint such as latency or energy. The difference is that NetAdapt gets there with a simple greedy loop instead of a learned agent: [Yang et al., §3] Each iteration aims to cut latency by a manually chosen amount ΔR. For each layer L k (A to Z), prune just that layer until its latency reduction meets ΔR, using a pre-built lookup table. Short-term fine-tune each candidate (10k iterations) and measure its accuracy. Keep the candidate with the highest accuracy. Repeat until the total latency reduction satisfies the constraint, then run a long-term fine-tune to recover accuracy. A bonus: every iteration produces a model, so you get a series of models with different costs (#models = #iterations). On the latency-accuracy plot, NetAdapt is 1.7× faster with 0.3% higher accuracy than the Multipliers baseline, and 1.6× faster with 0.3% higher accuracy than MorphNet. Approach How ratios are chosen Weakness Sensitivity analysis One layer at a time, then a threshold T Ignores interactions between layers AMC An RL agent (DDPG) outputs a ratio per layer Needs an RL training loop NetAdapt Greedy: prune the layer that hurts accuracy least, repeat Many short fine-tunes per iteration 6 · Fine-tuning turns a damaged model into a good one Back to your opening guess. On AlexNet, pruning without retraining loses about 0.5% accuracy at 50% pruned and over 4% at 80%. The weight histogram shows why: pruning cuts out the band of weights near zero. If you then retrain the remaining weights , the accuracy comes back, and you can push to roughly 90% pruned with no loss. [Han et al., Fig. 5] Train connectivity normal training Prune connections 50% → 70% → … Train weights LR × 1/10 to 1/100 Loop the last two steps: iterative pruning The learning rate for fine-tuning is usually 1/100 or 1/10 of the original. The network is already close to a good solution and only needs small corrections. Iterative pruning treats one prune plus fine-tune as an iteration and raises the target sparsity each time (50%, then 70%, …). On AlexNet, iterative pruning boosts the pruning ratio from 5× to 9× compared with one aggressive pruning step. So the answer to the opening question is closer to 90% , provided you prune gradually and retrain in between. Concept map Needs first Weights vs activations Loss function, L0 norm Lp norms, Hessian ReLU This topic Pruning Granularity Criterion Ratio Fine-tuning Leads to 2:4 sparse GPUs AMC / AutoML NetAdapt On-device AI From Relation To Pruning formalized-by arg min L s.t. ‖W P ‖ 0 < N Channel pruning is-a coarse-grained (structured) pruning Neuron pruning is-a coarse-grained weight pruning Magnitude pruning example-of OBD with equal curvature h ii Uniform shrink contrasts-with per-layer (non-uniform) ratios Sensitivity analysis requires a threshold T N:M sparsity enables ~2× speedup on Ampere GPUs Iterative fine-tuning causes 5× → 9× on AlexNet Exam check: try before you open Write the pruning objective and name every symbol. Answer arg min W P L(x; W P ) s.t. ‖W P ‖ 0 < N. L is the training loss, x the input, W P the pruned weights, ‖·‖ 0 the count of nonzeros, and N the target number of nonzeros. Prune [[4, −1], [−2, 3]] by 50% with row-wise L2. Answer Row norms are √17 and √13, so prune row 1: [[4, −1], [0, 0]]. Element-wise pruning would instead keep 4 and 3. Why does fine-grained pruning get high compression but little real speedup? Answer The zeros are scattered, so dense hardware still processes the full matrix shape. Turning sparsity into speed needs index handling or special hardware. Structured pruning leaves a smaller dense matrix instead. How many index bits does each kept value need in 2:4 sparsity, and why? Answer 2 bits: each kept value records its position among the 4 slots. There are C(4,2) = 6 possible patterns per group. State the three OBD assumptions and the resulting formula. Answer The loss is nearly quadratic (drop the cubic term), training has converged (drop the gradient term), and deletions are independent (drop the cross terms). The result is δL i ≈ ½ h ii w i ². A channel has APoZ 14/32. Another has 11/32. Which do you prune? Answer The 14/32 channel. A higher APoZ means it outputs zeros more often, so it is less important. What does the AMC reward return when the constraint is violated, and why use DDPG? Answer It returns −∞. DDPG is used because the action, a pruning ratio in [0,1), is continuous. What is the main weakness of sensitivity analysis, and which methods address it? Answer It ignores interactions between layers. AMC and NetAdapt search over the whole network, through RL or a greedy loop with short fine-tuning. What this does not show This page sticks to what the slides cover. It skips how sparse weights are actually stored and executed (sparse formats, compilers), pruning of large language models, and the specific reward and state encodings in the AMC paper beyond the slide summary. The Lab 4 curves are approximations traced from a plot, not measured data. All benchmark numbers depend on their hardware, as stated: Ampere GPUs for 2:4 sparsity and a Galaxy S7 Edge for the AMC latencies. References CSC 4814/6814 Efficient AI, Lectures 4–6 (Dr. Haoxin Wang, GSU) The course slides this page follows: formulation, granularity, criteria, sensitivity analysis, AMC, NetAdapt and fine-tuning. Lectures 4 and 5 are in the same folder. Han et al., Learning both Weights and Connections for Efficient Neural Networks (NeurIPS 2015) Magnitude pruning, the train → prune → retrain loop, the AlexNet curves, iterative pruning, and the compression table. Mao et al., Exploring the Regularity of Sparse Structure in CNNs (CVPR-W 2017) The fine-grained → channel-level granularity spectrum. Mishra et al., Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks (NVIDIA, 2021) 2:4 structured sparsity on Ampere, the compressed format with 2-bit indices, and the accuracy table. Liu et al., Learning Efficient Convolutional Networks through Network Slimming (ICCV 2017) Scaling-based pruning with trainable per-channel factors. LeCun et al., Optimal Brain Damage (NeurIPS 1989) The second-order Taylor criterion and its three assumptions. Hu et al., Network Trimming: A Data-Driven Neuron Pruning Approach (2016) APoZ: pruning neurons by their average percentage of zero activations. He et al., Channel Pruning for Accelerating Very Deep Neural Networks (ICCV 2017) Regression-based channel selection with β, solved by alternating between β and W. He et al., AMC: AutoML for Model Compression and Acceleration on Mobile Devices (ECCV 2018) Non-uniform vs uniform pruning, the RL formulation, ResNet50 density and MobileNet latency results. Yang et al., NetAdapt: Platform-Aware Neural Network Adaptation (ECCV 2018) The iterative ΔR loop, the lookup-table latency, short- and long-term fine-tuning, and the model series.
